extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical mechanics/hydrostatics (physics or engineering)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of foundational principles, assumptions, and empirical criteria used in statics and the statics of fluids (hydrostatics), with historical notes and experimental justification. The page explains what counts as valid principles, definitions (e.g., force), and the principal laws for liquids (buoyancy, pressure distribution, compressibility, Pascal's law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of well-considered observations
rubrics_metrics.description: One well-considered and tested observation is as good as another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles need not be established by multiple different historical derivations; once a principle is well considered and tested, it can be accepted without re-deriving it from earlier or roundabout observations. This serves the economy of thought and insight (aesthetics of science).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise a principle as the key to a domain
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise a principle (e.g., statical moments) as the key to the understanding of all the facts of a department, rather than deducing it awkwardly from unobvious propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After an initial historical derivation is performed once, both science and the individual are free to adopt the more convenient point of view that regards the principle as fundamental and uses it directly in explanation and problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'mania for demonstration' / mistaken rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive insistence on demonstration can produce a rigor that is false and mistaken; earlier deductions are sometimes given unwarranted authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks often exhibit this mistaken rigor; classical deductions (e.g., some renderings of Archimedes or Bernoulli) may appear more certain than they actually are. One should be critical of demonstrations that give a spurious impression of superior certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive knowledge is experimental and revisable
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctive knowledge, though enjoyed with exceptional confidence, is ultimately experimental knowledge and must give place to clearly and deliberately observed principles when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not regard instinctive or 'a priori' knowledge as immune to revision; such knowledge confronts us as irresistible but is still subject to failure when new regions of experience open up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical relation and contingency of principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The true relation and connection of different principles is historical: one principle may extend farther in some domains and another in others; no assurance exists that any single principle will always remain supreme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles single out aspects of the same facts more or less arbitrarily; one must not treat current principles as definitively completed or final if that will hinder the advancement of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of force in statics
rubrics_metrics.description: Force is any circumstance of which the consequence is motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statics investigates the modes of conjunction of such circumstances that result in no net motion. Force is characterized by direction (the direction of motion it alone would produce), point of application (the point whose motion is determined when freed from connections), and magnitude (that weight which acting in the given direction and at the given point produces the same motion or equilibrium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes of a force (direction, point of application, magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The direction of the force is the direction of the motion it would alone produce; the point of application is the point whose motion is still determined by the force when freed from connections; the magnitude is the weight which acting in that direction and at that point produces the same motion/equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other modifying circumstances that alone cannot produce the motion (virtual displacements, lever arms, etc.) are collateral conditions determinative of motion and equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use measurable weight as index for forces
rubrics_metrics.description: All circumstances determinative of motion (forces) may be represented and measured by quantities that stand for weight; measurable weight serves as a convenient and communicable index analogous to a thermometer for heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This substitution allows objective comparisons and quantitative treatment of forces in mechanical research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedean assumption on liquid pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is assumed as the essential property of a liquid that in all uniform and continuous positions of its parts the portion that suffers the lesser pressure is forced upwards by that which suffers the greater pressure."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This basic assumption underlies the classical derivation of buoyancy and the behavior of fluids in equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' principle of buoyancy
rubrics_metrics.description: A body immersed in a liquid loses weight equal to the weight of the liquid displaced; a body of the same specific gravity as the liquid will just completely submerge and supply by its weight the pressure of the displaced water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument illustrated by considering parts of a spherical (fluid) Earth and comparing weights of pyramidal elements; practical conception: immersed body behaves as if on a balance with displaced liquid on the other pan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stevinus' principle: solidification of fluid in equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: The solidification of a fluid in equilibrium does not disturb its equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this assumption follows that a mass of water immersed in water loses its whole weight; imagining submerged surfaces solidified (superficies), the upward pressure equals the weight of displaced water. This leads to laws such as pressure on the base being independent of vessel form and behavior of communicating vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of virtual displacements to liquids (Galileo / Pascal)
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of virtual displacements can explain equilibria in communicating vessels: displacements of columns are inversely proportional to areas and weights, and with appropriate handling yields Pascal's conclusions on pressure propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galileo used virtual displacements but omitted center-of-gravity considerations; Pascal used the principle more correctly by considering only surface pressures and showing that pressure on a superficial portion is propagated undiminished to every other superficial portion (illustrated by pistons loaded in proportion to their areas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental property of liquids: mobility of parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquid particles yield to the slightest pressure and therefore a fluid element can retain its shape only if the same perpendicular pressure be exerted on all its sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometrical reasoning shows why in equilibrium equal perpendicular pressures must act on all sides of a fluid element; this distinguishes fluids from solids and underpins hydrostatic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressibility of liquids (volume change proportional to pressure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liquids suffer through pressure a diminution of volume which is proportional to the pressure exerted per unit area; volume and density vary proportionally with pressure changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier belief in incompressibility was overturned by experiments (Canton, Oersted, Grassi); compressibility is small but measurable (Grassi: ~5 in 100,000 per atm at 0°C for boiled water).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure isotropy in a fluid at rest without external forces
rubrics_metrics.description: When equilibrium subsists in a liquid, in the interior of which no forces act and gravity is neglected, the same equal pressure is exerted on each and every equal surface-element however and wherever situated; pressure is the same at all points and independent of direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposition follows from considering the mobility and compressibility of parts; though perhaps not proven by extremely exact experiments, experience strongly supports it and it explains many phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure increases with depth under gravity (hydrostatic law)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a heavy liquid in equilibrium under gravity, the pressure increases proportionally to the depth beneath the surface (dp/dh = s, so p = h s if surface pressure is zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by considering a small rectangular parallelepiped element and balancing weight against pressure difference on top and bottom; only the gravity direction contributes to pressure increase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level surfaces and their relation to gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Points in a liquid at which the same pressure acts form level surfaces; displacements at right angles to gravity keep pressure unchanged, so level surface elements stand at right angles to the direction of gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagining the Earth fluid and spherical, the level surfaces are concentric spheres; level surfaces serve as diagrams of the force relations (used in analytical hydrostatics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure on base independent of vessel form
rubrics_metrics.description: The pressure on the base of a vessel depends only on the area of the base, the depth (height) of the fluid above it, and the specific gravity of the fluid: P = A h s; it is independent of the vessel's shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained via Stevinus' idea of solidified fluid replacing vessel walls: walls deform until their elasticity equilibrates the fluid pressure; practical implication: two vessels with same base area and height exert the same base pressure regardless of overall shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical demonstrations (Pascal's experiments) validating hydrostatic laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Various experiments (e.g., a glass tube with metal disc, mercury columns in siphons, leather bag tied to a tube) illustrate that immersion to sufficient depth supports discs by pressure, mercury rises in siphons due to pressure differentials, and objects can be forced into arms of tubes by pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These simple experiments demonstrate that pressure acts independently of direction, increases with depth, and can perform mechanical work (support discs, raise mercury), confirming theoretical propositions.
